lesson.title: Addressing with Respect
lesson.subtitle: Using 3rd-person verbs with usted: ¿cómo está usted? vs ¿cómo estás?

hook.title: The '-s' Switch
hook.content: Because he, she, and usted all share the exact same 3rd-person verb form (está, es, quiere, desea), speakers often include the word usted in questions (¿Cómo está usted?, ¿Qué desea usted?) so the listener knows you are addressing them rather than talking about someone else!

pattern.title: Comparing Informal and Formal Side by Side
pattern.content:
Informal tú: ¿Cómo estás? / ¿Qué quieres? / ¿Hablas español?
Formal usted: ¿Cómo está usted? / ¿Qué quiere usted? / ¿Habla usted español?

exercises.prompt: Match each English expression with its Spanish partner:
exercises.target_answer: estás, está usted, eres, es usted, quieres, quiere usted
exercises.meaning: you are (tú, state), you are (usted, state), you are (tú, identity), you are (usted, identity), you want (tú), you want (usted)
exercises.explanation: Removing the -s from estás/quieres gives the formal usted verb.

exercises.prompt: You are speaking to an older stranger on a train. Which question is polite?

exercises.idea: ask a lady politely how she is: 'How are you, madam?'

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.explanation: ¿Qué desea usted? — what you will hear in every Spanish shop and restaurant.

summary.outcome: Convert informal tú questions into formal usted questions by dropping the verb's final -s.

use_example.german: ¿Qué desea usted, señor? — Quiero un café, por favor.
use_example.english: What would you like, sir? — I want a coffee, please.

summary.takeaway: tú keeps the -s (estás, quieres); usted drops the -s (está, quiere).
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next ([902] The Politeness Toolkit): master muchas gracias, por favor, buenos días, and buenas tardes.

twist.explanation: ¿Es usted de Madrid? uses es (ser) for origin.

tú.etymology_derivation: Latin tū — the ancient Indo-European second person singular, preserved in Shakespeare's thou.

usted.etymology_derivation: Vuestra Merced ('Your Mercy') worn down over centuries to usted. Takes 3rd-person verb forms.

estás.context_translation: How are you? (How do you stand?)

está.etymology_derivation: Latin stat ('he/she stands') → está. Accent on the á keeps the stress on the tail.

es.shift_rule: Latin est — identical to English is
es.etymology_derivation: Proto-Indo-European *h₁ésti → Latin est → Spanish es. Sibling to English is.

querer.etymology_derivation: Latin quaerere ('to seek, ask for') evolved in Spanish to 'to want' and 'to love'. When you make an inquiry in English, you are asking what you want.

desear.etymology_derivation: Climb the English register ladder from 'want' to 'desire' and Spanish desear is waiting.

señor.etymology_derivation: Latin senior ('older') — English senior and sire.

señora.etymology_derivation: Takes el/la when talking ABOUT them (el señor García), and no article when addressing them directly.
